elements.element: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction.
elements.evidence: § 12.4 as rendered now reads "Customer may develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory," replacing the 24-month post-term worldwide non-compete; § 12.3 independently confirms "Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete... commitment." No other operative restriction on Customer's products, fields or territories remains.

elements.element: The restriction covers only a named competing product.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no restriction survives at all after the edit, so the narrowing requirement is vacuously satisfied — the preferred (no-restriction) outcome exceeds this fallback limit.

elements.element: The restriction applies during the term only.
elements.evidence: No restriction remains in § 12.4 or elsewhere, so there is no post-term tail; the element's condition is inapplicable.

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: The 24-month post-term duration was deleted and no replacement period exists; with zero duration the 12-month cap is not exceeded.

elements.element: The restriction permits Customer's internal development.
elements.evidence: § 12.4 expressly permits Customer to "develop... any product or service that competes with Vendor," and § 12.3 confirms nothing restricts Customer from developing any product or service.
§ 12.4 expressly permits Customer to "acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory"; § 12.3 likewise preserves acquisition freedom.

reasons: Preferred level is complete: the sole preferred element is met because the operative non-compete in § 12.4 has been converted into an affirmative permission, leaving no non-compete or field-of-use restriction binding Customer anywhere in the cited language.

Minimality holds: the edit touches only § 12.4, the single clause containing the offending restriction, and reuses that clause's own vocabulary ("develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory") rather than importing new procedures, survival tails, or extra obligations. § 12.3 — favourable existing language — is retained verbatim.

A residual observation, not a defect: the retained § 12.3 already states that nothing restricts Customer and that no non-compete commitment was made, so the rewritten § 12.4 is arguably confirmatory rather than strictly necessary. Because § 12.4 previously contained the operative restriction, editing it in place (rather than deleting it and leaving a numbering gap or an ambiguous silence) is a reasonable minimal repair and is consistent with, not duplicative in an operative sense of, § 12.3.

Intent is preserved: removing the restriction eliminates the direct contradiction with § 12.3 rather than creating one; no defined term is orphaned, no cross-reference dangles, and unrelated allocation, timing, remedies, and commercial mechanics (including the § 13.4 acceptable-use terms) are untouched.

Margin comment is compliant with tone and structure: it states what changed, why, cites the playbook position, and offers the fallback (single named competing product, term only, 12-month cap, internal-development and acquisition carve-outs) without lecturing.
Deterministic evidence corroborates the substantive read: the operation applies, no open-ended compete restriction on Customer remains, and both the minimality and element-coverage gates pass.
